questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had already been staying as well as studying in Istanbul and wanted to experience Ankara, both as a representative of "something else" in Türkiye (as opposed to Istanbul, where most people go) and of course due to it being the capital city.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I'm studying Turkish language and for this, Hacettepe Üniversitesi is a great university in many ways. Their TÖMER language course is intense and rewarding. Looking at my stay more generally, I believe I would have been able to meet, benefit and enjoy Ankara and the city's cultural and social aspect of it if the country hadn't been so severely hit by the earthquake in February.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I wasn't part of a regular introduction since the Türkiye/Syria earthquake happened on the night of my arrival, resulting in all universities cancelling international students and relocating all classes to zoom. However, the international office as well as the Erasmus+ coordinator was very helpful. Sometimes up to slow reply time can however occur.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had been told that I would follow regular university courses, but upon arrival I learned that I in stead would be following the intensive language course aimed at non-Turkish scholarship students. To get introduced to this, I had a meeting with the former as well as current Erasmus-coordinator, and was enrolled into the former coordinator's spring class as a kind of extra thing. From there the coordinator followed me to the TÖMER department, where I was told when to come and do a placement test. They asked me to come the next day where a class was doing their mid-way exam in B1. After this I just kept coming, nothing to worry about at all. Everybody were kind and attentive.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Ankara is not the easiest if you don't know anybody. I stayed in an airbnb, which is not a bad idea but BE AWARE that you'll need a contract to apply for student visa. I had a really great host who put me on his cotnract, but I don't think you can just expect this, so if you're doing airbnb you should check this in advance. Furthermore, for airbnbin Ankara, I gotta say 1) the opportunities aren't great, and 2) the longer you stay the more you understand how extremely overpriced the airbnb "rent" is. 

If you know anybody, definately ask for help. There are facebook-groups but you need to know somebody to let you in and also just to let you know which groups are nice. The groups will be called something like a district name or  feature the name of a university appealing especially to these universities' students. While I was there there were no active groups in English or with names including the word Ankara, so unless you're familiar with the language or the city, you really need to know someone. 

I've heard that the neighbourhood "100. yil" should be preferred by a lot of students and Bahcelievler looks cute.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Kizilay is the official center but consider wether you really want to live in the commercial center. I did it and I would suggest something else, it's unnecessarily crowded and messy in my opinion.

There is a metro going to Hacettepe, so as long as you're kinda close to that, you'll be fine. Taxis are cheap compared to Denmark and the so-called "dolmus" (minibusses) and regular busses make it alright to cross the city, though the busses don't really adhere to any particular schedule. There is an app where you can track the busses though, it's called "EGO Cep'te".

If you can find something close to a park or something green you'll appreciate it in the long run, since the city can be quite dense with main roads, metros and closely built apartment complexes.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I'm giving the "housing for students" a low point because it was difficult for me and I had nobody to help me.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My Turkish class, TÖMER,  wasn't "academic", it was pure language, but it was very good. You buy the book online and get it approximately one week later. Until then you can get by using online versions or prints. In class the only language spoken is Turkish, I don't even think my yeachers knew English, so it's hard core but it's the intention and it works. We had class every day from 9-14:30 with a one hour lunch break. The course is a logical and dynamic mix of introduction of new words and concepts, grammar, listening, reading, watching, writing, practice organized under theme shaped chapters (like "Entertainment", "Travel", "Love", etc). We did B1, B2 and C1 in the four months I was there and we were around 5-10 people in class.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Turkish class was way more intense at Hacettepe University than at UCPH. Only speaking Turkish, always learning new topics, gramatical constructions and relatively long days make up the intensity. I would say that you have to study outside of class to keep up, but we very rarely had homework, and in that sense you can also choose how much energy you want to put into it. You have to pass the class to continue to the next level though. The semester ends with a big exam and you get a diploma.

The one "normal" academic class I followed had the title "Avrupa'da Türkçe" and I took that more out of interest and curiosity than as a course I could contribute to and exel in. The level seemed a bit lower, but it is difficult to say. The course was probably 4 ECTS and was 2 x 40 minutes weekly, not all weeks had readings.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The teachers I met were extremely pedagogical at TÖMER, I guess since they are used to having very young people at around 17-21 yrs old. Its also inherently personal to learn a language, so except for the heaviness of the learning curve, it sometimes felt more like being in kindergarten.

I don't think I can say a lot about the teaching style in "Avrupa'da Türkçe" since it was zoom. It was always slide show based and we never had essays or presentations, only occational readings that you could get away with not reading if you wanted to.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Getting your student visa.
- I paid around 350 TL for the special health care insurance made in Türkiye that is mandatory to apply.
- Then maybe 50 TL to get biometric photos (remember to get them scanned and sent to you, otherwise the application website won't accept it
- Then 1500 TL to my airbnb host to get our passports verified, the contract verified, etc etc. 
OBS! The economy changes quickly in TR so these prices definately don't apply anymore, it is just to give you an idea. :-) I probably spent around 100€ on visa.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I was happy that you could take the comfortable train to Istanbul for like 280 TL (at that point like 70 DKK/9 EUR) each way, or to Konya or wherever.

Additional comments:
questions.answer: Never found anything due to campus being closed after the earthquake.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There is probably more that I just never had an opportunity to discover but: library, football field, stadium, tennis courts, running court, small lake, small forest, a range of cafées.

There weren't really any social or cultural stuff going on while I was there.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I don't know.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Of course Ankara is worth exploring. I especially liked the old town in Ulus and the museums. It rained a lot of the late spring so I never hung out a lot in the parks. And then students should visit other cities in Turkey. Istanbul is 4,5 hrs away with train, Konya 1,5. Izmir is 10 hrs with bus. I wish I had travelled more east too, there is so much to see.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I don't find Türkiye in itself difficult to adjust to. There are a lot of prejudice surrounding the country, but you can pretty much find you group of people there, no matter wether you're into museums, bar hopping, study groups or field trips. Of course there are more socially conservative and islamic sentiment, but I doesn't really affect your everyday life, like how you dress, eat or interact. Expect to receive attention from men if you are a woman, especially travelling alone, wearing something eye catching or come across as an "open person". Learn to tell them off.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Unfortunately no, not really. Going to cultural events, I would say, the few people I met I met like that. In general, the students never came to Ankara since they could attend university online instead, but that being said, young (and old) Turks are pretty chill and open to talk to.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: As mentioned above: certain special treatments as a women. I've lived in TR for two years and now 5 months in Ankara and I've never had anything actually bad happen to me -- but it can still be intense. Men talking to you on the bus, on the restaurant, in a bar, stuff like that. Develop a strategy and remember that it isn't you who should be feeling bad or embarrassed.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: All the other people who are super kind - being in a country where you can dive into majestic roman and islamic architecure - the fooood omg - the literature, so much cheaper there, even in translation

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Remember to explore the campus, wether to enjoy the nature or to find the art departments buzzing workshops
2) Don't postpone getting your documents ready for the visa, you will probably encounter something unexpected
3) Go to every event that attracts your attention to meet people and see new places, on or off campus, because Ankara is the local's city.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Not for my host institution maybe, but for Ankara: 
Read books or watch movies on Türkiye, if you haven't already. I read Ahmet Hamdi Tanpinar and Elif Shafak while I was there and it really adds depth to the otherwise foreign impressions.

Also, getting an insurance was really tricky for me. Every office I found on google or saw on a sign where magically non-existent when I arrived. When you find a place, stress that you need an insurance for the student visa application (ikamet) when getting an insurance. It shouldn't be more than around 15€. I almost paid 180€ because they didn't knew what I meant. If nothing else, go to TİMURLAR SİGORTA GENEL MÜDÜRLÜK by Kocatepe Camii, I got my insurance there.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Learning Turkish for real.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The loneliness and extreme lifeless-ness of the city caused by the state of the country after the earthquake.
